questions.stem: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay that begins with the sentence "As is known to all, gaining a sound knowledge of the basics is of vital importance for students to master an academic subject.” You can make comments, cite examples or use your personal experiences to develop your essay. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words ( not including the sentence given ).
questions.analysis:
【参考范文】
As is known to all, gaining a sound knowledge of the basics is of vital importance for students to master an academic subject. Just as a towering building cannot stand firm without a solid foundation, no student can reach academic heights unless the fundamentals are first laid down. The basics are not the trivial part of learning; they are the very ground on which deeper understanding is built.

In my own experience, this truth was made vivid when I began studying programming. At first I was eager to write fancy applications and skipped the elementary concepts of variables and loops. As a result, whenever a bug appeared, I had no idea where to look, and my code collapsed completely. It was only after I went back and mastered these basics that I could finally trace errors and write reliable programs. This lesson taught me that shortcuts around the fundamentals lead nowhere.

It follows that students should never underestimate the value of the basics. Rather than rushing toward complicated tasks, we ought to devote patient effort to consolidating the fundamentals first. Only by standing on such firm ground can we climb steadily toward true mastery of any subject.

sections.note: 听力为历年真题原文，题目与答案为官方标准答案；在线音频由语音合成朗读原文，不是考场录音；换浏览器、换手机都能播。

transcript.text: M: Hello, doctor.
transcript.zh: M：你好，医生。

transcript.text: W: Hello, please take a seat. I have your test results here, and it's good news. The blood test came back clear. There is no indication of any digestive issues.
transcript.zh: W：你好，请坐。我这里有你的检查结果，而且是个好消息。血液检查结果正常，没有任何消化系统问题的迹象。

transcript.text: M: So then why do I feel so poorly all the time?
transcript.zh: M：那我为什么总是感觉这么不舒服？

transcript.text: W: It's probably due to overwork and stress.
transcript.zh: W：这可能是过度劳累和压力造成的。

transcript.text: M: No, it can't be. I've always been working hard, but I've never felt stress. Other people suffering complain about that, but I don't. It must be something else.
transcript.zh: M：不，不可能。我一直都很努力地工作，但从来没有感到过压力。其他饱受压力折磨的人会抱怨这个问题，但我不会。一定是别的原因。

transcript.text: W: What you have just described is a common sentiment. Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise it. You told me you often work long into the night, right?
transcript.zh: W：你刚才描述的情况很常见。许多承受压力的人都没有意识到自己正处于压力之中。你告诉过我，你经常工作到深夜，对吧？

transcript.text: M: Yes, most days in fact. But I've been doing that for about 20 years now.
transcript.zh: M：对，实际上大多数日子都是这样。但我这样已经有大约20年了。

transcript.text: W: That doesn't matter. You could have been suffering from stress for 20 years without knowing it, and now it's catching up to you.
transcript.zh: W：那并不代表什么。你可能在不知情的情况下承受了20年的压力，现在它开始影响你了。

transcript.text: M: But what about my feeling tired all the time and not being able to sleep well at night?
transcript.zh: M：可是我总是感到疲惫，晚上也睡不好，这又是怎么回事？

transcript.text: W: Those are common consequences of stress. And if you don't sleep well, then of course you will feel fatigued. I'm going to prescribe some special sleeping pills for you. They have a soft, gentle effect and are made from natural ingredients, so your stomach should tolerate them fine, and there shouldn't be any negative side effects. Take one with your dinner and come see me after a month. If there is no improvement, I'll give you something stronger.
transcript.zh: W：这些都是压力带来的常见后果。如果你睡不好，当然就会感到疲劳。我会给你开一些特殊的安眠药。它们药效温和，是用天然成分制成的，所以你的胃应该能够很好地耐受，也不应产生任何负面副作用。晚餐时服用一片，一个月后再来见我。如果没有改善，我会给你开药效更强的药。

transcript.text: M: Thank you, doctor.
transcript.zh: M：谢谢你，医生。

transcript.text: W: That's not all. You should try and work less. Is there any way you can decrease your workload?
transcript.zh: W：还不止这些。你应该试着少工作一些。你有没有办法减轻自己的工作量？

transcript.text: M: Um, I'd have to think about it. I'm a restaurant manager and this industry is very competitive. There are many things to keep track of and stay on top of.
transcript.zh: M：嗯，我得考虑一下。我是一名餐厅经理，而这个行业竞争非常激烈。有很多事情需要跟进并确保掌控。

transcript.text: W: I recommend you think about delegating some responsibilities to someone else. I'm not asking you to retire just to slow down a bit. It's for your own health.
transcript.zh: W：我建议你考虑把一部分职责委派给其他人。我不是让你退休，只是让你稍微放慢节奏。这是为了你自己的健康。

questions.stem: What do we learn about the man from his test results?

options.text: It is clear that he is expected to enjoy a healthy life.
There is nothing wrong with his digestive system.
There is some indication of an issue with his blood circulation.
He doesn't know he has long been suffering from poor health.

questions.analysis: 细节题。答案句（P2）：The blood test came back clear. There is no indication of any digestive issues.信号：医生宣布结果的直接陈述句 。医生一坐下就直接通报结论 The blood test came back clear 并补一句 There is no indication of any digestive issue…

optionAnalysis.C: 原词陷阱：录音查的是 blood test 与 digestive issues，an issue with his blood circulation 借用了“血液 blood”的耳熟感，却把对象偷换成 blood circulation（血液循环），录音从未说循环有问题，且结果是 clear（清白），与“有问题”正好相反。 借用原文：You could have been suffering from stress for 20 years without knowing it
optionAnalysis.A: 过度推断：录音只说某项检查没问题，It is clear that he is expected to enjoy a healthy life 却推到“可望享有健康人生”——录音里他正feel poorly、被诊断有压力，谈不上健康一生，是无中生有的拔高。
optionAnalysis.D: 答非所问：He doesn't know he has long been suffering from poor health 套用了后文“压力潜伏二十年而不自知”的影子，但本题问的是 test results（化验结果），结果恰恰是“清白”，并未说明他长期体弱，错位安插。
optionAnalysis.B: 正确项：与答案句同义替换（no indication of any digestive issues ↔ nothing wrong with his digestive system “没有消化问题迹象”=“消化系统没毛病”）

questions.evidenceText: The blood test came back clear. There is no indication of any digestive issues.

questions.stem: What does the woman think is a common phenomenon among many people?

options.text: Mistaking symptoms of illness for stress.
Being unaware of the stress they are under.
Suffering from illness without recognising it.

questions.analysis: 细节题。答案句（P6）：What you have just described is a common sentiment. Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise it.信号：含 common / Many people 的概括句 。女方用 a common sentiment 与 Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise i…

optionAnalysis.D: 偷换概念：Suffering from illness without recognising it 与答案句框架一致（都是“X 而不自知”），但 X 被换成 illness；录音说的是 suffer from stress fail to recognise it——没认出的是压力不是疾病，差的正是那个核心变量。 借用原文：It's probably due to overwork and stress
optionAnalysis.A: 与原文相反：Mistaking symptoms of illness for stress 是“把病当成压力”，而录音是“有压力却没认出（把压力当别的）”，方向恰好反过来；男方原话是 I've never felt stress，是不承认压力，不是错把病当压力。
optionAnalysis.B: 原词陷阱：Complaining they are being overworked 蹭了录音 overwork and stress 的 overwork，但女方说的是很多人“没意识到压力”，恰恰不是“抱怨过劳”；男方甚至说 other people complain，他自己不抱怨，与“很多人抱怨”相反。
optionAnalysis.C: 正确项：与答案句同义替换（Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise it ↔ Being unaware of the stress they are under “承压却没认出”=“没意识到自己身处压力”）

questions.evidenceText: What you have just described is a common sentiment. Many people who suffer from stress fail to recognise it.

questions.stem: What does the woman say she will do for the man?

options.text: Explain to him the common consequence of stress.
Buy some sleeping pills for him from the drugstore.

questions.analysis: 细节题。答案句（P10）：I'm going to prescribe some special sleeping pills for you.信号：I'm going to + 动词的将来表态句 。女方用 I'm going to prescribe some special sleeping pills for you 主动声明下一步动作——I'm going…

optionAnalysis.D: 原词陷阱：Buy some sleeping pills for him from the drugstore 盗用了原句的 sleeping pills，却把动作从“医生开处方 prescribe”改成“去药店买 buy from the drugstore”；录音里医生是开方，不是替他去药店买药。 借用原文：Those are common consequences of stress
optionAnalysis.C: 答非所问：Explain to him the common consequence of stress 蹭了录音 Those are common consequences of stress，但那是医生在解释失眠成因，不是回答“她将为他做什么”这一动作；本题要的是她接下来要做的事，是开药。
optionAnalysis.B: 未提及：Give him another physical check-up 录音从未提及再做体检——医生是看着已有的 test results 直接开药，并约一个月后复诊，没有安排再次体检。
optionAnalysis.A: 正确项：与答案句同义替换（prescribe some special sleeping pills ↔ Prescribe some medication for him “开安眠药”=“开药（medication）”）

questions.evidenceText: I'm going to prescribe some special sleeping pills for you.

questions.stem: What does the man say about the industry he is engaged in?

options.text: It proves to be quite profitable.

questions.analysis: 细节题。答案句（P13）：I'm a restaurant manager and this industry is very competitive.信号：this industry is very + 形容词的直接评价句 。男方自陈身份后用 this industry is very competitive 直接评价所在行业——this industry is ver…

optionAnalysis.A: 原词陷阱：It calls for responsible management 蹭了男方自报身份 I'm a restaurant manager 里的 manager/management，但他评价行业用的词是 competitive，从没说这行“需要负责任的管理”，是借身份词造的干扰。
optionAnalysis.B: 未提及：It proves to be quite profitable 谈盈利，但男方对行业的描述只有“竞争激烈”和“事务繁多”，从未提到赚钱与否，是无中生有。
optionAnalysis.C: 未提及：It is remarkably promising 说行业前景可观，但录音里男方谈的是竞争和繁忙、并被建议放慢节奏，全无“前景大好”之意，属凭空添加的正面评价。
optionAnalysis.D: 正确项：与答案句同义替换（this industry is very competitive ↔ It is full of competition “非常有竞争性”=“充满竞争”）

transcript.text: W: Today on People in the News, our guest is John Williams. The name may not sound familiar to you, but John was once an acclaimed basketball player. John, you stunned fans by leaving the sport at just 25. Why did you retire so early?
transcript.zh: W: 欢迎收看今天的《新闻人物》，我们的嘉宾是约翰·威廉姆斯。这个名字大家可能不太熟悉，但约翰曾经是一位备受赞誉的篮球运动员。约翰，你在年仅25岁时退役让球迷们大吃一惊。你当时为什么这么早就选择退役呢？

transcript.text: M: Meg, I loved being an athlete, but I didn't love being a celebrity. I was in the limelight when I was still a high school student and went professional right after high school graduation, which was a mistake. I was a shy kid and I wasn't ready for all the media attention.
transcript.zh: M: 梅格，我热爱成为一名运动员，但我不喜欢成为名人。我还在上高中时就处于聚光灯下，高中一毕业就转为了职业球员，这其实是个错误。我当时是个害羞的孩子，还没做好应对所有媒体关注的准备。

transcript.text: W: But walking away from millions of dollars at the height of your career, most people wouldn't be able to resist the lure of such a high salary. When you left the sport, there was speculation that you were having issues with your teammates or even an injury.
transcript.zh: W: 但在职业生涯鼎盛时期放弃数百万美元，大多数人都无法抵挡如此高薪的诱惑。当你离开赛场时，外界曾推测你是和队友产生了矛盾，甚至是有伤在身。

transcript.text: M: Not at all. It was hard to quit. I was tempted to stay in the game, because I love basketball and I loved my team. As for money, I turned professional at 18. So I'd actually earned a lot and saved most of it, because I had great financial advisers. I knew basketball wasn't a career with a lot of longevity for most players, so I wanted to change careers while I was still young.
transcript.zh: M: 完全不是这样。选择放弃确实很难。我当时也纠结过要不要留下来继续打球，因为我热爱篮球，也热爱我的球队。至于钱的问题，我18岁就转为了职业球员。因为我有优秀的理财顾问，所以我实际上已经赚了不少钱，并且存下了大部分。我知道对大多数球员来说，篮球并不是一项能打很久的职业，所以我希望趁自己还年轻转换职业。

transcript.text: W: Okay, that was 20 years ago, and you're back in the news. You've created a foundation that works to get more kids playing team sports. Why?
transcript.zh: W: 好的，那是20年前的事了，现在你又重回大众视野。你创立了一个基金会，致力于让更多孩子参与团队运动。这是为什么呢？

transcript.text: M: I went to university and I studied public health and learned about the seriousness of the obesity epidemic, particularly among kids and adolescents in poor communities. I've spent the last two decades trying to alleviate the problem. The foundation is just the latest attempt.
transcript.zh: M: 我读了大学，学习了公共卫生学，了解到肥胖流行问题的严重性，尤其是在贫困社区的儿童和青少年群体中。在过去二十年里，我一直在努力缓解这个问题。这个基金会只是我最新的尝试。

transcript.text: W: The foundation uses private donations to support basketball teams for girls and boys in primary school, right?
transcript.zh: W: 这个基金会利用私人捐款来资助小学的男女生篮球队，对吗？

transcript.text: M: Actually, we support teams for secondary school students, too, and also have some public funding.
transcript.zh: M: 实际上，我们也资助中学生的球队，而且我们也有一些公共资金。

I was a shy kid and I wasn't ready for all the media attention.信号：被问者应答 + 转折 but 见真意 。主持人问他为何退役，被问者亲口回答的这句就是答案句；其中 but I didn\'t love being a celebrity 的转折 but 之后才是真正的退役理由，前半…

transcript.text: 1 Kate Atkinson was born in York, England, in 1951.
She worked hard to gain her credentials as an author.
She studied English Literature at University in Scotland.
After graduating in 1974, she researched a doctorate on American Literature.
Later, she taught at the university she graduated from, and began writing short stories in 1981.
She began writing for women's magazines after winning the 1986 Woman's Own Short Story Competition.
Her first novel, Behind the Scenes at the Museum, won the 1995 UK Book of the Year award.
The book is set in Yorkshire and has been adapted for radio, theatre, and TV.

She has written two plays for a theatre in Edinburgh—the first was called Nice and the second Abandonment, performed as part of the Edinburgh Festival in August 2000. 2 Whatever genre Atkinson writes in, her books touch on the themes of love and loss and how to carry on.
They are always presented with ingenuity and a wicked sense of humor.
Her books tend to be populated by odd, sometimes sinful, and generally flawed eccentrics who become credible by virtue of being so fully realized.
Her books have frequently been described as comedies of manners.
That is to say, comedies that represent the complex and sophisticated code of behaviour current in fashionable circles of society, where appearances count more than true moral character.
A comedy of manners tends to reward its clever and deceitful characters, rather than punish their bad deeds.
The humor of a comedy of manners relies on verbal wit and playful teasing.

Simply put, adaptability is a skill employers are increasingly looking for.
When you spend time learning a new task rather than resisting it, your productivity goes up.
You can also serve as an example to your co-workers who may be having trouble adapting, and can help lead your team forward.
Strategy consultant, Dorie Clark, explains it to us this way.
"I'd say that adaptability is an important skill in the workplace because frankly, circumstances change.
Competitors introduce new products, economy might enter a recession, customer preferences differ over time, and more.
If you shake your fist at the sky and say why can't it stay the same, that's not going to do very much good.
Instead, you need to recognise when circumstances have changed, so you can take appropriate action based on what is, rather than how you wish the world would be.
That enables you to make more accurate, informed and effective choices." 2 Also, the workplace itself has been evolving.
Today's work culture and management style is often based on teamwork, rather than a rigid hierarchy.
Brainstorming, which requires creativity, flexibility, and emotional intelligence, is a typical problem-solving technique.
Employees who are unable or unwilling to participate will not easily move forward in the company.
Employees who are flexible demonstrate other skills too.
They can reprioritize quickly when changes occur and suggest additional modifications when something is not working.

transcript.text: What makes humans different from other species? Some philosophers argue it's morals or ethics, while some scientists assert it's our greater cognitive development. But I argue that the main difference is our desire to combat routine. This makes being creative a biological mandate, as what we seek in art and technology is surprise, not simply a fulfillment of expectations.
transcript.zh: 是什么使人类区别于其他物种？一些哲学家认为是道德或伦理，而一些科学家断言是我们更高的认知发展水平。但我认为，主要区别在于我们渴望对抗惯常模式。这使创造具有生物学意义上的必然性，因为我们在艺术和技术中寻求的是惊喜，而不只是满足预期。

transcript.text: As a result, a wild imagination has characterized the history of our species. We build intricate habitats, devise complex recipes for our food, wear clothes that reflect constant changes in fashion, communicate with elaborate signs, symbols, and sounds, and travel between habitats on wings and wheels of our own design. To satisfy our appetite for novelty, innovation is key. But who innovates?
transcript.zh: 因此，狂野的想象力贯穿了我们这个物种的历史。我们建造精巧复杂的栖息地，为食物设计复杂的食谱，穿着体现时尚不断变化的服装，用繁复的标志、符号和声音进行交流，还乘坐由我们自己设计的翅膀和轮子，在不同栖息地之间往来。为了满足我们对新奇事物的渴望，创新至关重要。但谁在创新？

transcript.text: Now, many people, both laymen and experts, believe that only geniuses innovate. But I believe that innovation is not something that only a few people do. The innovative drive lives in every human brain, and the resulting war against the repetitive is what powers the massive changes that distinguish one generation from the next. The drive to create the new is a trait of being human. We build cultures by the hundreds and tell new stories by the millions. We create and surround ourselves with things that have never existed before, while animals do not. But where do our new ideas come from?
transcript.zh: 如今，许多人，包括普通人和专家，都认为只有天才才能创新。但我认为，创新并不是只有少数人才会做的事情。创新的驱动力存在于每个人的大脑中，而由此产生的反重复之战，正是推动巨大变革的力量，使一代人与下一代人彼此不同。创造新事物的动力是人类特有的特征。我们成百上千地建立文化，以数百万计讲述新的故事。我们创造并置身于此前从未存在过的事物之中，而动物不会这样做。但我们的新思想究竟从何而来？

transcript.text: According to many, new ideas come from seemingly nowhere to great minds. From this perspective, new ideas are almost like magic. They come in a flash of inspiration to a select few. However, the reality is that, across the spectrum of human activities, prior work propels the creative process. We may think of innovation as being the result of inspiration or genius, but it's really the result of developing the ideas of others further. This happens in technology, where one invention enables or inspires further inventions. And it happens in the arts, as writers, composers, and painters use the work of previous artists in their own work. The human brain works from precedent. We take the ideas we've inherited and put them together into some new shape.
transcript.zh: 许多人认为，新思想会凭空出现在伟大思想家的脑海中。从这个角度看，新思想几乎像是魔法。它们以灵感闪现的方式降临到少数人身上。然而，现实是，在人类活动的各个领域，先前的工作推动着创造过程。我们可能认为创新源于灵感或天才，但实际上，它是进一步发展他人思想的结果。这种情况发生在技术领域：一项发明会促成或启发更多发明。在艺术领域也是如此，作家、作曲家和画家会将前辈艺术家的作品运用到自己的创作中。人类大脑以先例为基础运作。我们吸收继承而来的思想，并将它们重新组合成某种新的形式。

transcript.text: What is a true creator? Is a creator a genius who makes something out of nothing? No. Creators are simply humans who use what they inherit, who absorb the past and manipulate it to create possible futures. Thus, humans are creators as a rule rather than as an exception.
transcript.zh: 什么是真正的创造者？创造者是那个能从无到有创造出某种事物的天才吗？不是。创造者只不过是运用继承之物、吸收过去并加以改造，从而创造出未来可能性的人类。因此，人类通常都是创造者，而不是只有少数例外者。

transcript.text: Many dog owners would tell you that their dog somehow knows when they're ill or upset, and according to researchers who study dog cognition, those pet owners are right. Dogs do know when their human companions are having a rough time. Not only can your dog sense when you have a cold, but domestic dogs have shown an aptitude for detecting both much smaller mood fluctuations and far more serious physical conditions. This is because dogs are extremely sensitive to changes in the people they're familiar with, and illness causes change. If a person is infected with a virus or bacteria, for example, their odor will be abnormal, and dogs are able to smell that change even if the human can't, because dogs have a much more powerful sense of smell than humans.
transcript.zh: 许多养狗的人都会告诉你，他们的狗不知怎么就能察觉到自己生病或情绪低落；而根据研究犬类认知的研究人员所说，这些宠物主人是对的。狗确实知道它们的人类伴侣正经历艰难时期。你的狗不仅能察觉你感冒了，家犬还表现出了发现细微情绪波动以及更严重身体状况的能力。这是因为狗对熟悉之人的变化极其敏感，而疾病会引起变化。例如，如果一个人感染了病毒或细菌，他的气味就会异常；即使人类自己察觉不到这种变化，狗也能闻出来，因为狗的嗅觉比人类强大得多。

transcript.text: Researchers have also found that a person's mood, which can be an indicator of a larger illness, triggers a dog's sense of smell. Human emotions manifest physically in chemical signals that are emitted by the body, and dogs are able to smell those as well. Beyond smell, dogs gather information from a person's voice in order to sense changes.
transcript.zh: 研究人员还发现，一个人的情绪可能是更严重疾病的迹象，并会触发狗的嗅觉。人类的情绪会以身体释放出的化学信号在生理上表现出来，而狗同样能够闻到这些信号。除了嗅觉之外，狗还会从人的声音中获取信息，以察觉变化。

transcript.text: In 2014, researchers discovered that dogs have an area of the brain similar to one in humans that allows them to understand emotional cues in the tone of a speaker's voice, beyond what they'd be able to pick up from familiar words alone. A person's voice can also carry indicators of illness. What's not understood quite so well is what dogs understand about these changes. Humans send out lots of cues, but whether dogs know some of these cues mean illness isn't clear. What we perceive as concern on a dog's part might be more like increased curiosity or suspicion that something is wrong with us, and sticking close by is a great way to gather more information about the situation.
transcript.zh: 2014年，研究人员发现，狗的大脑中有一个区域与人类大脑中的某个区域相似，使它们能够理解说话者声音语调中的情绪线索，而不仅仅是从熟悉的词语中获取信息。一个人的声音也可能携带疾病的迹象。人们目前还不太清楚狗究竟理解这些变化到了什么程度。人类会发出许多线索，但狗是否知道其中一些线索意味着疾病，还不明确。我们认为狗表现出的关切，可能更像是它们对我们出了问题这一情况产生了更强的好奇或怀疑，而待在我们身边则是获取更多相关信息的好方法。

transcript.text: Some researchers assert dogs will one day help doctors diagnose diseases, as some dogs have already demonstrated the ability to detect an assortment of ailments, including diabetes and certain types of cancer. But those researchers concede that's probably in the distant future. For now, research suggests dog ownership can have an array of benefits in and of itself. Keeping a pet dog has been shown to bolster health and boost mood. Dogs also help people relax, and they can be a particular comfort to those with chronic diseases.
transcript.zh: 一些研究人员断言，狗有朝一日将帮助医生诊断疾病，因为有些狗已经展现出检测多种疾病的能力，包括糖尿病和某些类型的癌症。但这些研究人员也承认，那可能是遥远未来的事。目前的研究表明，养狗本身就能带来一系列益处。事实证明，饲养宠物狗有助于增进健康、改善情绪。狗还能帮助人放松，对于患有慢性疾病的人来说，它们尤其能带来安慰。

transcript.text: Earlier this month, the think-tank called Onward published a report, "A Question of Degree", which argues that degrees in the creative arts are not good value for money. Ministers, according to Onward, should "crack down on courses that offer extremely limited value for money to students ten years after graduation", restricting the ability of such courses to recruit new students, if the average graduate earns below the student loans payment threshold. Courses like science, technology, engineering, and math, and economics, where the average graduate earns a lot, should be favored.
transcript.zh: 本月早些时候，名为 Onward 的智库发布了一份题为《程度问题》的报告，认为创意艺术类学位的性价比不高。Onward 认为，部长们应当“严厉整治那些在学生毕业十年后仍只能为其提供极低性价比的课程”；如果此类课程的毕业生平均收入低于学生贷款还款门槛，就应限制这些课程招收新生。对于科学、技术、工程、数学以及经济学等专业，由于其毕业生平均收入较高，则应予以优先考虑。

transcript.text: The report provides insight into a government review which looks at how to reform technical education and how to ensure students get good value for money. At first glance, it might even seem like Onward have a point. According to their data, the majority of creative arts students earn less than 25,000 pounds a year, ten years after graduation. The average male creative arts students, indeed, apparently earn much less than they would, had they simply never gone to university. This isn't really good for anyone, and it's certainly no good for graduates, who are forced to endure a lifestyle where they can never save up, never buy a house, never hope to retire.
transcript.zh: 这份报告为政府正在进行的一项审查提供了参考，该审查旨在研究如何改革技术教育，以及如何确保学生获得良好的性价比。乍看之下，Onward 似乎确实有道理。根据其数据，大多数创意艺术类学生在毕业十年后年收入低于25,000英镑。事实上，据称创意艺术类专业的男性学生平均收入远低于他们如果当初根本没有上大学所能获得的收入。这对任何人来说都不利，对毕业生而言尤其如此，因为他们被迫忍受一种永远无法攒下钱、永远买不起房、永远不敢指望退休的生活方式。

transcript.text: Onward has identified a real problem. Creative arts graduates from top universities—like Oxford, with a high proportion of privately-educated students—have fairly good work prospects. Well, 40 percent of all graduates—regardless of their degree—are on less than 25,000 pounds a year, 5 years after graduation. This suggests that the problem isn't really to do with specific students studying specific degrees, but really with the economy as a whole. Regardless of what they've studied, young people find it hard to get ahead unless they're lucky enough to be born with successful parents.
transcript.zh: Onward 确实发现了一个真实存在的问题。顶尖大学的创意艺术类毕业生，例如牛津大学的毕业生，由于其中有很大一部分学生来自私立学校，因此往往拥有相当不错的就业前景。可是，所有毕业生中有40%——无论他们所学的是什么学位——在毕业五年后年收入低于25,000英镑。这表明，问题其实并不在于某些特定学生攻读某些特定学位，而在于整个经济状况。无论年轻人学了什么，除非他们足够幸运，出生在拥有成功事业的家庭，否则都很难取得进展。

transcript.text: If ministers want to make education pay for young people, they need to look beyond the higher education sector, towards the wider world. The rewards that education gives us are not measurable. They are not always instantly obvious, and certainly not always direct. An education makes you a different person from the one you would have been if you hadn't received it. We need to look at the value of education not in the context of a bank balance, but of a life. If we continue to allow ourselves to be distracted with talk of "value for money", we will all be made poorer as a result.
transcript.zh: 如果部长们希望让教育为年轻人带来回报，就需要把视野放在高等教育领域之外，转向更广阔的社会。教育带给我们的回报是无法衡量的。它们并不总是立刻显现出来，当然也并不总是直接的。接受教育会让你成为一个不同于未接受教育时的自己的人。我们需要从人生的角度，而不是从银行账户余额的角度，来审视教育的价值。如果我们继续让自己被“性价比”之类的说法分散注意力，最终我们所有人的生活都会因此变得更加贫乏。

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the hills of central Kenya, almost lime-green with the sparkle of tea bushes in the sunlight, farmers know all about climate change. "The rainy season is no longer predictable," says one. "When it is supposed to rain it doesn't, then it all comes at once." Climate change is an issue that will affect everyone on the planet. For Africans its consequences will be particularly bitter: whereas other regions were able to grow rich by burning coal and oil, Africa will pay much of the human price without having enjoyed the benefits. "Africa only represents 2% of global greenhouse-gas emissions but it is the continent that is expected to suffer the most from climate impacts," says Mafalda Duarte, who runs the World Bank's $8bn Climate Investment Funds.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Although there are huge uncertainties as to the precise impacts of climate change, enough is known to say that global warming represents one of the main threats to Africa's prosperity. Parts of the continent are already warming much more quickly than the average: temperatures in southern Africa have increased by about twice the global rate over the past 50 years. Even if the world were to cut emissions enough to keep global warming below 1.5℃, heat-waves would intensify in Africa and diseases would spread to areas not currently affected. Farming would also be hit hard. About 40% of the land now used to grow maize(玉米) would no longer be suitable for it. Overall, it is estimated that maize yields would fall by 18-22%.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Africa is particularly vulnerable, in part because it is already struggling to feed itself and it will have to vastly increase yields and productivity if it is to put food on the plates of a fast-growing population, even without climate change. The UN's Food and Agriculture Organisation reckons that by 2050 global food production would have to rise by about 70% over its level of 2009 to meet demand from a population that is growing in numbers and appetite. Much of this new demand will be in Africa. Yet the continent already imports about $50bn-worth of food a year and that figure is expected to more than double over the next five years. Self-sufficiency is not Africa's goal, but the fact that it spends more money importing food than it does buying capital goods suggests it has room for improvement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Finding out why is not hard. Most farms are tiny, ploughed by hand and reliant on rain. More than half of Africa's people make their living from farming. Although its total harvest has climbed over the past few decades, this is mainly because there are more people farming more land. But in many places there is no spare land to farm. Plots in Rwanda are so small that you could fit 250 of them onto the average American farm. And although output per worker has improved by more than half over the past 30 years in Africa, that is still far behind the 2.5 times improvement in Asia. Yields of maize are generally less than two tonnes per hectare, a fifth the level in America.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The low productivity of African farmers is reflected in national economic statistics—despite absorbing so much labour, farming generates just 15% of GDP. "They can't even feed their families," says Jennifer Blanke, a vice-president of the African Development Bank in charge of agriculture. "Farm productivity hasn't improved in many parts of Africa for 100 years."

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One reason is that in the first few decades of independence, many African governments neglected farming as they focused on industrialising their economies. Others damaged it by pushing down the prices that state monopolies paid for their crops in order to subsidise workers in cities with cheap food. Ghana taxed cocoa(可可粉) exports so heavily that production collapsed by half between the 1960s and 1980s, despite a jump in the global price of cocoa. Yet over the past two decades or so governments and donors have begun to look again at farming as a way of providing jobs for the 13 million young people entering the workforce each year. Much of the focus has been on getting small farmers to use fertiliser and, more important, better seeds. The results can be impressive. Improved varieties of sorghum(高梁), for instance, can produce a crop that is 40% larger than the usual variety. Infrastructure is important. A World Bank irrigation project in Ethiopia helped farmers increase their potato harvest from about 8 tonnes per hectare to 35 tonnes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Better techniques help, too. Small coffee farmers in Kenya are able to increase their incomes by 40% by following a few simple guidelines on caring for their bushes, such as trimming all but three of their stems. Many of their neighbours do not follow the advice, because it seems counter-intuitive. More stems ought to lead to more coffee beans, they say. Yet after seeing those following the advice get bigger harvests for a season or two, many others start doing the same.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One way of spreading knowledge is to link farms to big buyers of their harvests. When Diageo, a British drinks giant, built a brewery in western Kenya, it wanted to use local crops to make a beer cheap enough to compete with illicit home brew. It organised farmers into groups, improved supply chains for them to get seeds and fertiliser and then agreed to buy their grain. It now provides a market to about 17,000 farmers. Across the region it has doubled its use of local raw material to about 80% over five years, says John O'Keeffe, who runs its Africa business.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: An even more important change is the move from traditional farming to building businesses that can profitably bring technology and investment to small farmers. Taita Ngetich, a young Kenyan, was studying engineering when he wanted to earn a little money on the side. He scraped together 20,000 Kenyan shillings (about $200) to plant tomatoes. Everything went wrong. The crop was attacked by pests. "Then there was a massive flood that swallowed all our capital," he says. Mr Ngetich persevered by looking into buying a greenhouse to protect his plants from bugs and rain. The cheapest ones cost more than $2,500 each, so he designed his own for half the price. Soon neighbouring farmers started placing orders with him, and now his firm, Illuminum Greenhouses, has sold more than 1,400 greenhouses that provide livelihoods to about 6,000 people. The business does not stop there; he also supplies fertiliser, high-quality seedlings and smart sensors that increase yields.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Illuminum's success shows how technology can help even small farms become more productive. Because such a large share of Africa's population earns a living from agriculture, even small improvements in productivity can lift the incomes of millions of people. But over the longer run small-scale farming can go only so far, especially in the face of climate change and population pressure.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: "If we really want to lift people out of poverty we have to finance projects that will get them an income of at least $100 a month so that they can pay for health care and education," says Mr Ngetich. "Projects that give them an extra $2 a month from growing beans or maize aren't going to get them there." Getting those big jumps will need better jobs in factories and cities.

paragraphs.text: Unfortunately a new study in Nature Neuroscience makes for disheartening reading. The team finds that the majority of editors in top psychology and neuroscience journals are male and based in the United States: a situation that may be amplifying existing gender inequalities in the field and influencing the kind of research that gets published.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Men were found to account for 60% of the editors of psychology journals. There were significantly more male than female editors at each level of seniority, and men made up the majority of editors in over three quarters of the journals. Crucially, the proportion of female editors was significantly lower than the overall proportion of women psychology researchers.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The differences were even starker in the neuroscience journals: 70% of editors were male, and men held the majority of editorial positions in 88% of journals. In this case, the proportion of female editors was not significantly lower than the proportion of female researchers working in neuroscience—a finding that reveals enduring gender disparities in the field more broadly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Based on their results, the team concludes that "the ideas, values and decision-making biases of men are overrepresented in the editorial positions of the most recognized academic journals in psychology and neuroscience."

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Gender inequality in science is often attributed to the fact that senior academics are more likely to be male, because historically science was male-dominated: it's argued that as time goes on and more women rise to senior roles, the field will become more equal. Yet this study showed that even the junior roles in psychology journals tended to be held disproportionately by men, despite the fact that there are actually more female than male junior psychology faculty.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: This implies that a lack of female academics is not the problem. Instead, there are structural reasons that women are disadvantaged in science. Women receive lower salaries and face greater childcare demands, for instance, which can result in fewer publications and grants—the kinds of things that journals look for when deciding who to appoint. Rather than simply blaming the inequality of editorial boards on tradition, we should be actively breaking down these existing barriers.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: A lack of diversity among journal editors also likely contributes to psychology's WEIRD problem. If journal editors are largely men from the United States, then they will probably place higher value on papers that are relevant to Western, male populations, whether consciously or not.
